title: Massive performance degradation for complex query on PostgreSQL 16+
body: I maintain and develop Indico, and a statistics query that takes a few seconds on PostgreSQL 14/15 takes over three hours on our PostgreSQL 16.11 production database. With the supplied container reproducer, PostgreSQL 14 works, PostgreSQL 15 works when the container has increased shared memory, and PostgreSQL 16 and newer produce massive CPU and disk usage, so I stopped those reproducer runs early. I included EXPLAIN ANALYZE links from PostgreSQL 14 and 16, a compressed structure-and-dummy-data SQL file, and the problematic query. I am running PostgreSQL 18.3 on Linux for the reported reproduction.

symptoms_visible: My Indico statistics query takes only a few seconds on PostgreSQL 14 and 15, but it took more than three hours on our PostgreSQL 16.11 production database.
With the supplied reproducer, PostgreSQL 16 and newer start consuming massive CPU and tens of gigabytes of disk, so I stop the query rather than waiting for it to finish.
N0.label: N0 severe PostgreSQL 16+ regression reported

symptoms_visible: The query finishes normally on PostgreSQL 16 and 18 when I set work_mem to 128MB.
With work_mem still at 128MB, PostgreSQL 18 also finishes normally when I disable memoize.
N1.label: N1 memory and memoize probes completed

symptoms_visible: Using the updated larger dataset, PostgreSQL 14 finishes normally.
On PostgreSQL 16 with work_mem at 4MB, CPU and disk use rise rapidly and I abort after a few seconds; at 32MB the query completes.
N2.label: N2 comparable dataset and memory threshold established

symptoms_visible: The original query remains extremely slow and disk-intensive on my affected PostgreSQL 16 setup at low work_mem.
N3.label: N3 parallel hash batching explosion isolated

symptoms_visible: My affected production version still requires increased work_mem to avoid the multi-hour behavior; I have not tested a build containing the identified executor fix.
N4.label: N4 null-key hash-join fix identified

symptoms_visible: A maintainer reports that the original simplified query no longer fails on current master and that reverting the null-key hash-join change makes it fail again; I have not retested the fix on my own system.
N_terminal.label: terminal fix identified but reporter has not retested

question_patterns: Could you rerun the query on PostgreSQL 16 or newer with work_mem increased substantially and share the result?
Please try work_mem at 128MB to see whether the excessive disk activity and runtime change.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I set work_mem to 128MB and the query worked fine on both PostgreSQL 16 and PostgreSQL 18. Here are the EXPLAIN ANALYZE results: https://<redacted-host>/s/7Zan and https://<redacted-host>/s/H15B.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: At 128MB it still consumes tens of gigabytes of disk and does not finish in a reasonable time.
It also works at 96MB, while the default setting still exhibits the same slowdown.

question_patterns: What happens if you disable memoize and rerun the query?
Could you capture the plan with enable_memoize set to off?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: On PostgreSQL 18, with work_mem still at 128MB, it also worked with enable_memoize set to 0: https://<redacted-host>/s/SaVI.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: With 128MB it is a little faster when memoize is disabled, but both runs finish normally.

edges.comment: Reporter c1: these are handler-requested configuration probes. The raw outcomes show that more work_mem avoids the behavior; because the memoize run also used 128MB, it does not independently establish memoize as the cause.

question_patterns: Were the PostgreSQL 14 and 16 plans generated from the same data snapshot?
Can you explain the row-count difference between the plans?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Good catch: I generated the original test data from an older production copy rather than a recent one.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The PostgreSQL 14 and 16 plans came from completely different schemas and unrelated datasets.

question_patterns: Can you refresh the reproducer from a larger, current data copy and rerun the comparison?
Please provide comparable results using the same updated dataset.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I reran it with a larger database and replaced the compressed SQL file from my initial report with the latest one.

question_patterns: With the updated dataset, what happens on PostgreSQL 14 and on PostgreSQL 16 at low and moderate work_mem settings?
Could you compare the updated data at 4MB and 32MB of work_mem?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: PostgreSQL 14 completes normally. On PostgreSQL 16 at 4MB, CPU and disk usage become massive, so I aborted it after a few seconds. At 32MB it completes, and the plan is https://<redacted-host>/s/mYiY.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: With the same updated data, PostgreSQL 14 now has the same massive disk usage and slowdown as PostgreSQL 16.
The threshold is closer to 48MB rather than 32MB, but low work_mem still triggers the same behavior only on PostgreSQL 16.

edges.comment: Reporter c3: the reporter acknowledges the original snapshot mismatch, replaces the reproducer data, and provides new raw comparisons. The reporter also states that the same older copy was fast on 14/15 and bad on 16, so the snapshot mismatch does not explain away the version regression.

solution.intent: Reproduce the query independently, compare parallel and non-parallel execution, and inspect hash-join batching and temporary-file usage rather than treating increased work_mem as the root fix.
solution.concrete_example: Run the supplied scripts across PostgreSQL versions, repeat with parallel query disabled, inspect pg_stat_database and pgsql_tmp before and after execution, and instrument parallel hash batch growth.
solution.inference_hint: The reporter supplied the reproducer and memory-dependent outcomes. A maintainer independently measured roughly 1.5 seconds on PostgreSQL 14/15 versus about 156–162 seconds on 16–18 with parallelism, no comparable version regression with parallelism disabled, roughly two million temporary files and 70GB of temporary writes, and growth from an estimated 32 hash batches to 262144. These are maintainer-side measurements, not statements made by the reporter.

edges.comment: Maintainer c4-c5, not the reporter's system: Tomas Vondra reproduced the supplied scripts, isolated the behavior to parallel execution, measured the temporary-file explosion, and instrumented the parallel hash join's repeated batch growth. The evidence is represented as engineer-obtained information and is never put into the reporter's clarification answers.

solution.intent: Bisect the PostgreSQL 16 regression, minimize the query to the failing outer parallel hash join, and validate whether the existing null-join-key handling change prevents the runaway repartitioning.
solution.concrete_example: Bisect with the full query, reduce it to a forced parallel hash left join, compare variants that exclude null join keys, then test current master both with and without the hash-join null-key handling improvement.
solution.inference_hint: Maintainers traced the version boundary to the change that enabled additional outer joins in parallel hash joins, despite the original query containing no FULL JOIN. The minimized LEFT JOIN still fails when forced into a parallel hash plan. Current master succeeds, reverting the later hash-join null-key handling improvement restores the failure, and variants excluding null keys do not show that same failure. This supports null-key handling as the final accepted mechanism rather than the earlier tentative join-order explanation.

edges.comment: Maintainers c6-c10: Tom Lane suggested minimization and bisection; Tomas Vondra bisected and reduced the failure; Thomas Munro connected the case to the stop-partitioning logic and asked about the null-key handling change; Tomas confirmed current master was good and reverting that change restored the original failure. These are maintainer findings, not reporter-produced measurements.

solution.intent: Use a PostgreSQL build containing the parallel hash join null-key handling fix, retain higher work_mem only as a temporary workaround, and ask the reporter to verify the original query before declaring the production issue resolved.
solution.concrete_example: The multi-hour runtime is caused by a parallel hash outer join repeatedly repartitioning when null join keys prevent its stop-partitioning logic from taking effect, producing hundreds of thousands of batches and enormous temporary-file traffic. Test a build containing the hash-join null-key handling improvement against the original query; until such a build is available on the affected branch, increased work_mem can avoid the behavior as a workaround.
solution.inference_hint: The final root cause is not merely a planner join-order change or insufficient work_mem. The decisive maintainer evidence is the parallel-only failure, the growth to 262144 batches with enormous temporary-file traffic, the minimized parallel hash LEFT JOIN, the null-excluding variants, and the current-master/revert comparison. The thread ends before the reporter tests the fix or receives an answer about supported-branch backports.

edges.comment: Technical resolution from c9-c10, with reporter c11 establishing that no reporter-side verification occurred before the thread snapshot. The backport question is release coordination and remains unanswered, so no supported-version availability claim is scored or invented.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the final accepted root cause: a PostgreSQL 16-era parallel hash outer-join path can repeatedly repartition in the presence of null join keys, reaching hundreds of thousands of batches and causing extreme temporary-file, disk, CPU, and runtime growth.

Must ground the diagnosis in the surfaced evidence: the issue disappears when parallel execution is disabled, higher work_mem avoids it, the failing join grows to 262144 batches with roughly two million temporary files and about 70GB of temporary writes, and current master succeeds while reverting the null-key handling improvement restores the failure.
Must recommend testing or using a build containing the hash-join null-key handling fix; increased work_mem may be offered as a practical temporary workaround but not as the underlying fix.
Must not present memoize, ordinary data-size differences, or planner join order alone as the final root cause.
Must ask the reporter to rerun the original workload on a build containing the fix and must not declare the reporter's production issue verified or resolved before that retest.

persona_hint.experience_level: Experienced application maintainer and developer who can create large SQL reproducers, compare PostgreSQL versions in containers, change session settings, and interpret and share EXPLAIN ANALYZE results.
persona_hint.communication_style: Concise, technically precise, and cooperative; promptly runs requested tests, supplies links and updated datasets, acknowledges data mismatches, and asks practical questions about availability on supported PostgreSQL branches.
